Data Structure. Organized formats for storing and accessing data in memory, designed to enable efficient operations like searching, insertion, and deletion. From simple arrays to complex graphs, they form the foundation of computer science and are central to designing fast algorithms. The choice of data structure directly determines how quickly a program can solve a problem.

Arrays store elements in contiguous memory. They provide fast random access in constant time, but insertion and deletion are expensive operations. Linked lists use pointers to connect nodes. They offer flexible insertion and deletion in constant time if the position is known, but searching is slow, taking linear time. Stacks and queues are abstract structures imposing LIFO or FIFO ordering on data. These are often implemented on top of arrays or linked lists.

Trees organize data hierarchically. Binary search trees enable logarithmic time search if the tree is balanced. Graphs generalize trees by allowing arbitrary connections between nodes. They are essential for modeling networks and relationships. Hash tables map keys to values with nearly constant time average-case lookup. They use hash functions that distribute keys across buckets to achieve this performance.

Algorithms operate on data structures, and the choice of structure directly affects algorithm performance. The tree data structure is hierarchical and common in databases and search applications. Graph data structures are general structures for representing relationships. Arrays are the simplest and most fundamental data structure. Linked lists are an alternative to arrays with different performance tradeoffs. Hash tables enable fast key-value lookups.
